verdict.rationale: Four lexical patterns converge on the denial. Hebrews 9:27 sets death and judgment in an appointed sequence with 'is laid up or reserved' (apokeitai), plus 'once' (hapax), then 'and after this judgment' (meta touto krisis), so the stage after death is adjudication (a verdict being passed) not adjustment. Luke 16:26 fixes the gulf with 'has been fixed and remains fixed' (esteriktai, the perfect passive of sterizo, a tense marking a settled standing state), around the once-in-the-canon word 'chasm' (chasma, a hapax legomenon meaning a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible), with crossing declared impossible in both directions. Second Samuel 12:23 has David cease intercessory fasting at the child's death, reasoning the direction is one-way with 'return or bring back' (shuv). Paul's immediacy texts, 'to be away from the body and at home with the Lord' (ekdemesai ek tou somatos kai endemesai pros ton kyrion) in 2 Corinthians 5:8 and 'to depart and be with Christ' (analusai kai sun Christo einai) in Philippians 1:23, place the believer with the Lord at death without an intermediate alterable phase. The proposition is held with medium rather than high confidence because 2 Timothy 1:18 has Paul utter a wish-prayer in the optative mood (the classical mood expressing a wish), 'may he grant' (doe), for Onesiphorus seeking 'mercy on that Day' (eleos en ekeine te hemera), and the Protestant-canon corpus this query traverses does not include 2 Maccabees 12:44 to 46, the principal text outside this canon scope for the contrary practice.

scripture.reasoning: The clause sets death and judgment in a fixed appointed order. 'Is laid up or reserved' (apokeitai, the present passive form of apokeimai meaning to be laid up or reserved for) governs the human lot, qualified by 'once' (hapax), with 'to die' (apothanein), then the adversative continuation 'and after this judgment' (meta touto krisis). The single appointed death is followed by adjudication (a verdict being passed), not by a further window for revising the deceased state, so the lexical force is finality of the state after death. 'Is laid up' (apokeitai) occurs only four times in the canon (here, 2 Timothy 4:8 for the crown of righteousness, Colossians 1:5 for the hope laid up in heaven, Luke 19:20 for the mina laid up in a cloth), and each occurrence carries the sense of something set aside in a fixed reserved state.

Within the narrative on the lips of Abraham, 'a great chasm' (chasma mega), the only canonical occurrence of 'chasm' (chasma, a hapax legomenon meaning a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible), stands 'between' (metaxy) the two states, and 'has been fixed and remains fixed' (esteriktai, the perfect passive form of sterizo). The perfect tense (a completed action whose result still stands) marks a settled completed standing state still in force. Two verbs negate passage in both directions, 'so that those wishing to cross over cannot' (hopos hoi thelontes diabenai me dynontai) and 'nor do any cross from there' (mede ekeithen diaperosin), so that those wishing to cross cannot, and none cross from there. The wording encodes an irreversible separation after death, and the immediately following request from the dead rich man for Lazarus to be sent to his living brothers is denied, showing post-mortem petitions (requests from after death) themselves do not effect a change.

David explains his prior practice with the temporal clause 'while the child was still alive' (beod hayyeled chay), paired with 'I fasted and wept' (tsamti waevkeh). The fasting and weeping, the active entreaty (earnest request) to God on the child's behalf, are bounded by the child's living state. The Hebrew ties intercession (prayer on someone else's behalf) to the period before death, setting up the contrast in the next verse.

With the child now 'dead' (met), David asks 'why should I now fast' (lammah zeh ani tsam), and answers with the rhetorical 'can I bring him back again' (haukal lahashivo od). The verb 'return or bring back' (shuv) frames the irreversibility. The closing 'I am going to him but he will not return to me' (ani holek elav wehu lo yashuv elay) makes the direction one-way. David ceases all intercession (prayer on someone else's behalf) at death, treating the dead one's state as no longer subject to his entreaty.

Paul writes 'to be away from the body and at home with the Lord' (ekdemesai ek tou somatos kai endemesai pros ton kyrion). The verbs are aorist infinitives (the simple action 'to do' form), 'to be away from one's people' (ekdemeo) and 'to be at home with one's people' (endemeo), in a contrastive pair. The clause posits a direct transition from bodily life to presence with the Lord, with no intervening alterable phase named. The wording leaves no slot for a state after death subject to petition (request) from the living.

Paul says 'to depart and be with Christ' (analusai kai sun Christo einai), in a single coordinated infinitive pair governed by 'having desire' (epithymian echon). 'To loose or depart' (analuo), joined by 'and' (kai) to 'be with Christ' (sun Christo einai), presents departure as immediately conjoined to being with Christ. The comparative 'for it is by far better' (pollo gar mallon kreisson) ranks this state over remaining in the flesh. The grammar offers no temporal gap or alterable intermediate condition, reinforcing the immediacy pattern.

'The dead know nothing' (metim einam yodeim meumah), and the absence of further 'reward or wage' (sakar), in the under-the-sun perspective of Qoheleth (the speaker of Ecclesiastes), bound the active engagement of the deceased with the living world. Within the genre's horizon, the dead do not transact, which leaves no addressee within history for the living's entreaty (earnest request) on their behalf to alter. The text is hyperbole (deliberate overstatement for effect) within Qoheleth's frame but contributes to the canon's silence about reciprocal post-mortem petition (mutual exchange of requests with the dead).

Hezekiah's psalm says 'for Sheol does not thank you, death does not praise you' (ki lo sheol todeka mavet yehalleleka), with 'Sheol' (sheol, the realm of the dead in the Hebrew Bible) and 'death' (mavet) as the subjects of negated verbs of praise and acknowledgement. The wording denies an active Godward exchange from 'Sheol' (sheol, the realm of the dead) within this prayer's frame. This belongs to the Old Testament pattern in which the realm of the dead is silent toward God, which entails no canonical pathway for the living to mediate change there.

complicating_texts.resolution: Paul writes 'may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that Day' (doe auto ho kyrios heurein eleos para kyriou en ekeine te hemera). The verb 'may he grant' (doe) is tagged V-2AAO-3S in the TAGNT grammar code, that is aorist active optative third singular (the simple-action active form in the wish or hope mood, third person singular), the classical mood of a wish-prayer rather than a directive intercession (a commanded prayer on someone's behalf). The object is 'mercy' (eleos), and the temporal scope is 'on that Day' (en ekeine te hemera), the end-times judgment Day named 'Day' (hemera) elsewhere in the pastoral epistles (for example 2 Timothy 4:8 with the same 'is laid up' (apokeitai)). The text never states that Onesiphorus is dead. The deceased reading rests on inference from 2 Timothy 4:19 greeting his household alone, not on any explicit lexical datum. Even if the deceased reading is granted, the optative (wish or hope mood) seeks future end-times mercy at the Day of Judgment, which is consistent with finality at death rather than an alteration of any present post-mortem state. The wording here is genuinely ambiguous about the addressee's living/dead status, which is why the verdict is held at medium not high confidence.

The dead rich man petitions Abraham to send Lazarus to his living brothers, and the petition is denied. The passage thus depicts requests from the realm after death being refused and reinforces, rather than complicates, the finality pattern of verse 26.

This pericope (passage), Judas Maccabeus offering a sin-offering for the slain and the narrator's commendation of prayer for the dead, is the principal text appealed to for the contrary practice. It falls outside the Protestant 66-book canon and therefore outside the lexical store this query traverses (MACULA-Hebrew, MorphGNT, OSHB, STEPBible TAHOT/TAGNT, and ETCBC-BHSA all index canonical Hebrew and Greek). The pipeline cannot adjudicate the text directly from indexed morphology (word-form analysis) and lexicon (dictionary) data. The verdict is therefore canon-scoped, and a reader who accepts the deuterocanon (the additional books accepted by some traditions beyond the Protestant 66) would weigh this passage that this pipeline cannot weigh; the present analysis flags the gap rather than silently absorbing it.

variants.note: No variant units supplied in the bundle. Luke 16:26 carries minor witness variation in conjunction and pronoun forms marked in the SBLGNT text, but none touches 'has been fixed' (esteriktai), 'chasm' (chasma), 'between' (metaxy), or the negation of crossing, so the verdict on fixity holds across readings. Hebrews 9:27 is textually stable for 'is laid up' (apokeitai), 'once' (hapax, a word occurring only once in the entire Bible), and 'judgment' (krisis). 2 Timothy 1:18 is textually stable for the optative (wish or hope mood) 'may he grant' (doe), per NA28, NA27, Tyn, SBL, WH, Treg, TR, and Byz agreement in the STEPBible TAGNT editions field. ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) data has not been ingested for these books.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: finality-at-death (no warrant for prayers for the dead)
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Within the Protestant 66-book canon, Hebrews 9:27 orders death then judgment with 'is laid up' (apokeitai) and 'once' (hapax), Luke 16:26 fixes the chasm with the perfect (completed action whose result still stands) 'has been fixed' (esteriktai) and double negation of crossing, 2 Samuel 12:23 has David cease intercession at death with 'return or bring back' (shuv), and 2 Corinthians 5:8 plus Philippians 1:23 set the believer immediately with the Lord at death via 'to be away from / at home with' (ekdemeo/endemeo) and 'to depart and be with Christ' (analuo/sun Christo einai). The canon contains no verb predicating change of a state after death through living petition (request), and no narrative example of prayer for the dead succeeding. The proposition follows from the dominant lexical pattern.

A reading that admits prayer for the dead leans primarily on three lexical points the words themselves do not foreclose. First, 2 Timothy 1:18 has Paul use the wish-prayer optative (the mood expressing a wish) 'may he grant' (doe) with the object 'mercy' (eleos) for Onesiphorus, in a passage that never states he is alive; the silence is genuinely ambiguous. Second, the appointed-judgment texts speak to finality at the end-times Day, not directly to whether the intermediate state (the condition between death and final judgment) is altogether sealed from intercession. Third, the principal positive text appealed to historically, 2 Maccabees 12:44 to 46, lies outside the Protestant canon and therefore outside this lexical pipeline's scope; the words themselves are not in view, but a reader who accepts that book has a positive textual basis the pipeline does not survey. The reading is defensible within a wider canon, and the optative (wish or hope mood) in 2 Timothy 1:18 keeps the question genuinely contested even within the narrower canon.

hermeneutics.notes: Analogia scripturae (the practice of interpreting Scripture by other Scripture) links the Hebrew narrative of David ceasing entreaty (earnest request) at death with the Greek epistolary and gospel statements of appointed judgment, a fixed chasm, and immediacy with the Lord. Progressive revelation (the principle that later Scripture sharpens earlier Scripture) is mild here; the New Testament sharpens the post-mortem topography (the map of the realm after death) the Old Testament narrative assumes. The verdict's scope is the 66-book canon the lexical pipeline indexes; a wider-canon framework changes which texts are available to weigh, and the present file flags that boundary explicitly rather than smuggling it.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Examine whether the Hebrew and Greek of the 66-book canon supplies warrant for prayers offered on behalf of the dead and whether the deceased state is alterable after death or settled at death.
stem_audit.notes: The stem phrases 'lack biblical warrant' and 'the finality of judgment after death is settled at death' embed the conclusion (VERDICT-CHANGED: no, the conclusion stands but was derived neutrally). The verdict is derived from the neutral question whether the wording warrants such prayer or fixes the state, then reported against the original stem. The lexical pattern of appointed judgment, a fixed chasm, immediacy with the Lord, and David's cessation supports the original stem's direction within the canon this pipeline traverses, with the 2 Timothy 1:18 optative (wish or hope mood) and the deuterocanonical (extra-canonical, accepted by some traditions) 2 Maccabees 12:44 to 46 (out of scope here) supplying the genuine contestation.

lay_summary: Several passages in the Hebrew and Greek canon line up on this point. Hebrews 9:27 says people are appointed to die once, and the verb there, 'is laid up' (apokeitai), means is laid up or reserved, paired with 'once' (hapax, a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible), and then after this comes judgment. So the order is death, then a verdict, not death then a window for adjustment. Luke 16:26 puts a great chasm between the two states after death. The word for chasm, 'chasm' (chasma), appears only this once in the whole canon, and the verb for fixed, 'has been fixed' (esteriktai), is in the perfect tense (a completed action whose result still stands), which marks a settled, completed, still-standing condition. Two verbs then say crossing is impossible in both directions, and the dead rich man's own request is refused. In 2 Samuel 12, David fasts and weeps while his child is alive, but the moment the child dies he stops, asking whether he can bring the child back, using the verb 'return or bring back' (shuv), and saying he will go to the child but the child will not return to him. Paul adds two immediacy statements. In 2 Corinthians 5:8 he uses a pair of verbs, 'to be away from / at home with' (ekdemeo/endemeo), meaning to be away from the body and at home with the Lord, and in Philippians 1:23 he speaks of 'departing' (analuo) and being with Christ as one joined event. Read together, the words give no verb for changing a dead person's lot and no example of the living successfully petitioning to do so. The genuine contestation comes from two places. First, in 2 Timothy 1:18 Paul utters a wish-prayer, the optative mood (a verb form expressing a wish), 'may he grant' (doe), asking that Onesiphorus may find mercy on the Day of Judgment, and the text does not say whether Onesiphorus was alive or dead at the time, so the silence cuts both ways. Second, the main passage cited historically for prayer for the dead, 2 Maccabees 12:44 to 46, sits outside the Protestant 66-book canon and therefore outside the corpus this analysis surveys; a reader whose canon includes that book has a text this pipeline does not weigh. Within the canon this pipeline indexes, the lexical weight favors the proposition that the state after death is settled at death, with one ambiguous wish-prayer text and a canon-scope question that keep the matter contested at the edges.
